questionItems.concept: Expiratory time against a slowly emptying lung: how rate and inspiratory time decide the time left to exhale

unchangedForLegacyRecords.prompt: An obstructive patient still has outward flow when each new inspiration begins. What would shortening expiration tend to do?

choices.label: Increase the opportunity for gas trapping
Increase the time available for gas release
Reduce resistance in the tube and airways

changedWording.previous: Apply does the breath have time to finish? to a short authored case.
changedWording.current: See how a setting decides the time the lung has to empty, before judging whether a change helps.

changedWording.previous: Resistance and compliance influence how quickly the respiratory system empties. Expiratory flow still present when the next breath starts suggests incomplete emptying. The resulting intrinsic PEEP is additional to the set PEEP; a valid expiratory hold can help assess it.
Increase the opportunity for gas trapping. There is less time to empty a system that is already emptying slowly.
changedWording.current: Outward flow at the start of each breath means this lung has not finished emptying. For mandatory breaths, a higher rate shortens the cycle and the loss comes out of expiration; a longer inspiratory time at the same rate does the same. Less expiratory time leaves more volume behind, so the next breath starts higher and trapped volume and intrinsic PEEP can rise. More expiratory time or less obstruction helps the lung empty, although in severe obstruction flow can persist even with a long expiration.
After any change in rate or inspiratory time, look at expiratory flow at the moment the next breath starts; in a passive patient, a valid expiratory hold measures the intrinsic PEEP.

changedWording.previous: There is less time to empty a system that is already emptying slowly.
changedWording.current: Outward flow at the next breath already shows incomplete emptying. Less expiratory time leaves more of each breath behind, so trapped volume and intrinsic PEEP can rise.

changedWording.previous: Shorter expiration reduces, rather than increases, the available emptying interval.
changedWording.current: Shortening expiration means less time for gas release by definition. The reading is tempting because more breaths per minute can feel like more gas out, but each exhalation gets shorter.

changedWording.previous: Changing time does not itself remove an obstructing load.
changedWording.current: Timing and obstruction are separate levers. Shortening expiration leaves the obstruction in place; treating the obstruction is what lets gas leave faster.

questionItems.concept: Set PEEP against total PEEP: an expiratory hold reads what the lung holds, including intrinsic PEEP

unchangedForLegacyRecords.prompt: A valid expiratory hold shows pressure above set PEEP. What does that difference represent in this passive example?

choices.label: Extra pressure chosen on the PEEP control
The flow-resistive peak during inspiration
Intrinsic pressure remaining after expiration

changedWording.previous: Apply does the breath have time to finish? to a short authored case.
changedWording.current: Separate the PEEP you set from the pressure the lung actually holds at end-expiration.

changedWording.previous: Resistance and compliance influence how quickly the respiratory system empties. Expiratory flow still present when the next breath starts suggests incomplete emptying. The resulting intrinsic PEEP is additional to the set PEEP; a valid expiratory hold can help assess it.
changedWording.current: During an expiratory hold the valves close and flow stops. With nothing flowing, which pressure does the airway reading come to match?

changedWording.previous: Intrinsic pressure remaining after expiration. Intrinsic PEEP is pressure additional to set PEEP from incomplete emptying under these conditions.
changedWording.current: An expiratory hold closes the circuit at end-expiration. Once flow stops, airway pressure equilibrates with alveolar pressure, so the reading is total PEEP. Set PEEP is only the baseline the ventilator applies; the excess is intrinsic PEEP, from volume still trapped because expiration did not finish. For example, set PEEP 5 cmH₂O with a hold reading of 12 cmH₂O means intrinsic PEEP of about 7 cmH₂O. The number is interpretable only when the patient makes no inspiratory or expiratory effort during the hold and the pressure has had time to plateau, and it can underestimate trapping behind airways that close completely.
Compare it with the expiratory flow trace: flow still present when the next breath starts is the waveform sign of the same trapped volume.

changedWording.previous: The set PEEP is only the selected baseline; the excess was measured, not selected.
changedWording.current: The PEEP control sets the baseline the ventilator applies, and it has not changed. The console may display the higher total PEEP after the hold, but the excess was measured, not selected.

changedWording.previous: That describes a different phase and comparison.
changedWording.current: Peak pressure belongs to inspiration, when gas flows through the airways; its resistive part is the peak-to-plateau difference. An end-expiratory hold has no flow, so it contains no resistive pressure.

changedWording.previous: Intrinsic PEEP is pressure additional to set PEEP from incomplete emptying under these conditions.
changedWording.current: With flow stopped at end-expiration, the reading reflects pressure in the alveoli. The excess over set PEEP is intrinsic PEEP from gas that had not left before the next breath was due.

questionItems.concept: Dynamic hyperinflation as a circulatory emergency, and why raising the rate or the alarm limit makes it worse

unchangedForLegacyRecords.prompt: Another patient has high pressure, persistent expiratory flow at the next breath, and worsening hypotension. What is the most appropriate priority?

choices.label: Urgent bedside support and assessment of incomplete emptying
A higher mandatory rate to correct gas exchange promptly
A higher alarm limit while awaiting the next routine review

changedWording.previous: Apply one alarm, different patients to a short authored case.
changedWording.current: Recognize trapped gas that has become a circulatory problem, and why the quick fixes on the console make it worse.

changedWording.previous: Use the patient’s stability first, then valid pressure comparisons, expiratory flow, and effort. Ask which finding supports your explanation and which competing explanation remains. Reassess after an action using the same discriminating signals.
changedWording.current: Three findings arrive together. Which one explains the other two, and what does trapped volume do to blood returning to the heart?

changedWording.previous: Urgent bedside support and assessment of incomplete emptying. The pattern raises concern for dynamic hyperinflation affecting circulation. Respond under the local emergency protocol.
changedWording.current: Expiratory flow still present when the next breath starts shows incomplete emptying. As trapped volume builds, pressure in the chest rises, venous return and right-ventricular filling fall, and blood pressure can drop sharply. High airway pressure and hypotension with that flow pattern make dynamic hyperinflation the leading explanation, while other causes of high pressure with hypotension, such as tension pneumothorax, stay on the list. Treat it as a bedside emergency: get help, support the patient and assess emptying under your local emergency protocol.
Reassess the same signals after each action: whether expiratory flow now reaches zero before the next breath, whether intrinsic PEEP falls and whether blood pressure recovers.

changedWording.previous: The pattern raises concern for dynamic hyperinflation affecting circulation. Respond under the local emergency protocol.
changedWording.current: Flow still leaving at the next breath, rising pressure and falling blood pressure together point to trapped volume affecting the circulation. Getting help and assessing emptying treats the likely cause while the patient is supported.

changedWording.previous: Shortening expiration may worsen trapping and circulatory compromise.
changedWording.current: Tempting when gas exchange looks like the problem, but more breaths per minute shorten each expiration, and this patient is already failing to empty.
A higher rate shortens every expiration, so more gas is trapped, pressure in the chest rises further and blood pressure can fall further. Correcting CO₂ is not the immediate threat here.

changedWording.previous: Changing an alarm boundary does not treat an unstable patient.
changedWording.current: An alarm limit changes when the ventilator warns you, not what is happening in the chest.
Raising the limit silences a warning while trapped volume and hypotension continue, and a routine review is too slow for an unstable patient.

questionItems.concept: Breath count is not effective ventilation, and oxygen fraction does not clear CO₂

unchangedForLegacyRecords.prompt: A patient with rising CO₂ has a high total rate and persistent outward flow before every new breath. Which interpretation is most defensible?

choices.label: A high rate proves adequate CO₂ clearance
Incomplete emptying may limit effective ventilation
A higher oxygen fraction will directly clear the CO₂

changedWording.previous: Apply what will change the co₂? to a short authored case.
changedWording.current: Keep breath count, effective ventilation and oxygen fraction apart when CO₂ is rising.

changedWording.previous: Alveolar ventilation is the portion of ventilation reaching gas-exchanging lung. CO₂ also depends on production. A rate change alters breath timing promptly, but a blood-gas response takes time; in obstruction, more rate may worsen trapping instead of improving effective ventilation.
changedWording.current: CO₂ leaves with gas that reaches exchanging lung and then gets out. What does the expiratory trace say about how much gets out before each breath?

changedWording.previous: Incomplete emptying may limit effective ventilation. The expiratory pattern means a further rate increase could worsen trapping.
changedWording.current: CO₂ is set by its production relative to alveolar ventilation, not by the number of breaths. Here flow is still outward when each breath starts, so every breath begins from a larger trapped volume. Adding rate would shorten expiration further and add to trapping, and the expected fall in CO₂ may not follow. Oxygen fraction acts on oxygenation, not on CO₂ clearance.
Compare exhaled tidal volume and total rate with expiratory flow at each breath start, and measure intrinsic PEEP with a valid hold when the patient is passive.

changedWording.previous: Rate alone does not establish effective alveolar ventilation.
changedWording.current: Rate counts breaths, not the gas that reaches exchanging lung and leaves it. A high rate with incomplete emptying can coexist with rising CO₂.

changedWording.previous: The expiratory pattern means a further rate increase could worsen trapping.
changedWording.current: Outward flow at every breath start shows incomplete emptying. More rate would shorten expiration further, so the expected fall in CO₂ may not follow.

changedWording.previous: Oxygen fraction is not a direct control of alveolar ventilation.
changedWording.current: Oxygen fraction sets how much oxygen each breath carries; it does not increase alveolar ventilation, so it cannot clear CO₂. In some patients with COPD, extra oxygen can even raise CO₂.

questionItems.concept: A control changes its own variable: FiO₂ is an oxygenation lever, distinct from PEEP and from ventilation

unchangedForLegacyRecords.prompt: FiO₂ is increased with PEEP unchanged. Which statement describes what was directly changed?

choices.label: The pressure maintained between breaths
The oxygen fraction in inspired gas
The effective volume clearing CO₂

changedWording.previous: Apply did oxygenation improve at a cost? to a short authored case.
changedWording.current: Name what a single control changes directly, and keep the patient’s response as a separate observation.

changedWording.previous: FiO₂ changes oxygen concentration at the airway. PEEP changes end-expiratory pressure and may help maintain aerated lung; it can also overdistend lung or affect circulation. Improved saturation is one result, not the whole reassessment.
The oxygen fraction in inspired gas. FiO₂ changes concentration; improved blood oxygenation remains a patient response to assess.
changedWording.current: Raising FiO₂ changes one thing directly: the oxygen fraction of every breath, on the oxygenation side. Whether saturation or PaO₂ improves is the patient’s response, which you still check. It is not the pressure between breaths, which is PEEP and did not change, and it is not the ventilation that clears CO₂, which belongs to the other column.
Watch saturation or PaO₂ for the response and read CO₂ separately; in some patients with COPD, extra oxygen can raise CO₂ indirectly.

changedWording.previous: That describes the PEEP setting, which was unchanged.
changedWording.current: That is PEEP, and the stem keeps PEEP unchanged. PEEP and FiO₂ are both oxygenation levers, which is why they are easy to confuse.

changedWording.previous: FiO₂ changes concentration; improved blood oxygenation remains a patient response to assess.
changedWording.current: FiO₂ changes the oxygen concentration of every breath. Whether blood oxygen improves is a patient response that still has to be checked.

changedWording.previous: Changing oxygen fraction does not directly increase alveolar ventilation.
changedWording.current: Tidal volume, rate, emptying and dead space set CO₂ clearance. Changing the oxygen fraction does not increase alveolar ventilation.

questionItems.concept: Rising CO₂ with acceptable saturation: work from the determinants of CO₂, not the oxygen numbers

unchangedForLegacyRecords.prompt: CO₂ is rising while saturation remains acceptable. Which assessment best addresses the CO₂ problem?

choices.label: Delivered ventilation, emptying, and metabolic demand
Oxygen concentration and the saturation alarm limit
Airway cuff pressure and the humidity setting

changedWording.previous: Apply what will change the co₂? to a short authored case.
changedWording.current: Work the CO₂ problem with the quantities that set CO₂, even when the oxygen numbers look reassuring.

changedWording.previous: Alveolar ventilation is the portion of ventilation reaching gas-exchanging lung. CO₂ also depends on production. A rate change alters breath timing promptly, but a blood-gas response takes time; in obstruction, more rate may worsen trapping instead of improving effective ventilation.
changedWording.current: Saturation and CO₂ answer different questions. Which quantities decide how much CO₂ leaves the lung each minute?

changedWording.previous: Delivered ventilation, emptying, and metabolic demand. CO₂ reflects effective alveolar ventilation relative to production. Emptying constrains a rate change.
changedWording.current: Arterial CO₂ reflects CO₂ production relative to alveolar ventilation, the part of each minute’s ventilation that reaches gas-exchanging lung. So the check has three parts: whether the breaths are delivered as set (exhaled tidal volume and total rate), whether the lung empties before the next breath and whether CO₂ production has risen. Acceptable saturation shows oxygen transfer is adequate on the current settings; it says nothing about whether ventilation is keeping up with CO₂.
Check exhaled tidal volume against the setting, then expiratory flow at the next breath start, before changing rate or tidal volume.

changedWording.previous: CO₂ reflects effective alveolar ventilation relative to production. Emptying constrains a rate change.
changedWording.current: These are what set CO₂: the gas actually delivered, whether it can leave before the next breath and how much CO₂ the patient produces.

changedWording.previous: Those primarily concern oxygenation and monitoring, not CO₂ clearance.

questionItems.concept: Breath delivery is not oxygen transfer: shunt and ventilation–perfusion mismatch

unchangedForLegacyRecords.prompt: A patient receives regular supported breaths, but oxygen transfer remains poor. Which interpretation best explains this possibility?

choices.label: Gas movement and oxygen transfer are different steps
Regular breath timing confirms effective oxygen transfer
Outward gas movement prevents oxygen from reaching blood

changedWording.previous: Apply follow one supported breath to a short authored case.
changedWording.current: Separate a ventilator that is delivering breaths from a lung that is exchanging gas; this is the first form of the oxygenation-versus-ventilation distinction.

changedWording.previous: A ventilator helps move gas into the respiratory system. A signal starts inspiration, support is delivered, inspiration ends, and gas flows out. Moving gas supports breathing; oxygen transfer and CO₂ removal still depend on the patient’s lungs and circulation.
changedWording.current: The ventilator can only deliver gas to the airways. What has to happen after the gas arrives for oxygen to reach the blood?

changedWording.previous: Gas movement and oxygen transfer are different steps. Ventilation moves gas; transfer into blood also depends on the lung and circulation.
changedWording.current: A ventilator moves gas in and out of the airways. Oxygen reaches the blood only in lung units that receive that gas and are also perfused. When units are collapsed or flooded, blood passes them without picking up oxygen (shunt), and poorly matched units add to the deficit. In respiratory failure on the ventilator, this ventilation–perfusion problem, rather than breath delivery, is the usual cause of hypoxemia, so regular timing shows delivery, not adequate oxygen transfer.
Read the oxygenation levers and response — FiO₂, PEEP, saturation or PaO₂ — separately from breath delivery; the oxygenation section compares them directly.

changedWording.previous: Ventilation moves gas; transfer into blood also depends on the lung and circulation.
changedWording.current: Delivering breaths moves gas to the airways; oxygen transfer also needs lung units that are both ventilated and perfused. Either step can fail while the other works.

changedWording.previous: Timing describes breath delivery, not whether oxygen reaches the blood.
changedWording.current: Tempting because the ventilator looks as if it is doing its job, but timing describes delivery only. Collapsed or flooded lung can receive regular breaths and still not transfer oxygen.

changedWording.previous: Expiration is a normal part of breathing; it is not itself evidence of failed oxygen transfer.
changedWording.current: Expiration happens in every breath, including in patients whose oxygenation is normal, so it cannot explain why this patient’s oxygen transfer is poor.

questionItems.concept: Two clocks: breath timing changes at once and arterial CO₂ later, so check delivery and emptying before escalating

unchangedForLegacyRecords.prompt: The rate has just changed. Breath timing changes promptly, but a blood-gas response is not yet available. What is the best next interpretation?

choices.label: The rate change has already failed to affect CO₂
A repeat rate increase is needed immediately
Mechanical effects need review before judging gas exchange

changedWording.previous: Apply what will change the co₂? to a short authored case.
changedWording.current: Keep two clocks apart: the breath changes on the next cycle, the blood gas later.

changedWording.previous: Alveolar ventilation is the portion of ventilation reaching gas-exchanging lung. CO₂ also depends on production. A rate change alters breath timing promptly, but a blood-gas response takes time; in obstruction, more rate may worsen trapping instead of improving effective ventilation.
changedWording.current: Which effects of the change can you verify on the screen now, and which need time before they mean anything?

changedWording.previous: Mechanical effects need review before judging gas exchange. First observe delivery and emptying, then assess gas exchange after an appropriate clinical interval.
changedWording.current: A rate change alters breath timing on the next cycle, but arterial CO₂ moves to its new level more slowly, so an early or missing blood gas cannot show whether the change worked. What can be checked now is mechanical: whether the new rate is delivered, whether exhaled tidal volume held and whether expiratory flow still reaches zero before each breath. Judge CO₂ on a blood gas taken after an appropriate interval, then decide whether a further change is needed.
Confirm delivered rate and exhaled volume, look at end-expiratory flow for new trapping, then plan when to repeat the blood gas.

changedWording.previous: A prompt mechanical change and a later gas response occur on different time scales.
changedWording.current: Breath timing changed at once, but CO₂ takes longer to settle, so no result yet is not evidence that the change failed.

changedWording.previous: Escalating before checking delivery and emptying can cause harm; no failure has yet been established.
changedWording.current: Tempting when CO₂ is the goal, but nothing yet shows the first change was insufficient.
Stacking a second rate increase before the first has settled, and before checking emptying, can create trapping and hypotension while the CO₂ benefit is still unknown.

changedWording.previous: First observe delivery and emptying, then assess gas exchange after an appropriate clinical interval.
changedWording.current: Delivery and emptying can be checked now; gas exchange is judged on a blood gas taken after an appropriate interval.
